itinerary.cal: Best climbed July-September, once the Hannegan Pass road is snow-free and Challenger Glacier crevasses are more consolidated; a North Cascades NP wilderness permit is required for the Perfect Pass/Whatcom Pass zone and is worth reserving ahead in peak season.

days.note: From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (3,110 ft), a good trail climbs to Hannegan Pass (5,066 ft) then drops to the Chilliwack River crossing (~2,750 ft, 9 mi in). From there it's a steep, viewless climb back up onto Easy Ridge to a camp near 5,800-6,000 ft with big Picket Range views.
days.title: Hannegan Pass to Easy Ridge camp
days.objective: Reach a bivy on Easy Ridge

days.note: Traverse Easy Ridge past the old lookout site, then drop through the notch known as 'imperfect pass' near Whatcom Peak and fight back up talus/heather to Perfect Pass (6,300 ft) - one of the best bivy sites in the range and the standard staging camp for both Mount Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle.
days.title: Easy Ridge to Perfect Pass high camp
days.objective: Establish base camp at Perfect Pass

days.note: An early alpine start to cross the Challenger Glacier (~3 mi) to the base of the pinnacle's dike-streaked shield, then 4 pitches of rock (5.9, 5.8, 5.8, 5.7) up the face and ridge crest to the summit, before reversing the route and re-crossing the glacier back to camp. Parties often continue the same long day to tag Mount Challenger's main summit as well.
days.title: Climb Poltergeist Pinnacle via the Challenger Glacier

itinerary.totalNote: A remote 4-day expedition (~35 mi round trip, ~10,000+ ft cumulative gain) out of the Hannegan Pass trailhead; Poltergeist Pinnacle itself is a single technical add-on day climbed from a Perfect Pass high camp during a broader Mount Challenger trip.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FS Road 32; Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk — standard access point for Mount Challenger/Picket Range approaches via Hannegan Pass Trail #674.
waypoints.directions: Drive Forest Road 32 to its end, where the Hannegan Pass Trailhead sits at about 3,120 ft and Trail #674 starts. A Northwest Forest Pass is required, and there is a kiosk at the parking area. Plan the trip for July through September, once the Hannegan Pass road is snow-free and the Challenger Glacier crevasses are more consolidated. A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is required for the Perfect Pass/Whatcom Pass zone and is worth reserving ahead in peak season.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass
waypoints.note: Maintained trail ends at the pass crest; leave it here and drop east into the Chilliwack River valley to pick up the unmaintained Easy Ridge climbers' path toward Perfect Pass.

waypoints.name: Imperfect Impasse (Easy Ridge)
waypoints.note: Steep, often wet and slippery down-climbing slabs above a deep gorge on Easy Ridge — the cross-country crux of the approach and a common turnaround point in poor conditions.

waypoints.name: Perfect Pass
waypoints.note: Established high bivy on the ridge crest between Easy Ridge and Mount Challenger; the standard base camp for Challenger and Poltergeist Pinnacle climbs (alternative to a Luna Cirque camp).

waypoints.name: Challenger Arm gap
waypoints.note: Traverse around Challenger Arm to gain the edge of the Challenger Glacier; rope up for glacier travel here.

waypoints.name: Challenger Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Roped travel across open crevasses on the Challenger Glacier; the well-trodden track runs roughly 3 miles from Perfect Pass/Challenger Arm to the base of Poltergeist Pinnacle.

waypoints.name: Base of Poltergeist Pinnacle (East Face dihedral)
waypoints.note: Leave the glacier at the pinnacle's base; the East Face route starts in a short technical dihedral system just left of the dike-streaked shield feature.

waypoints.name: Poltergeist Pinnacle
waypoints.note: Small, exposed summit block on the southernmost of the subsidiary pinnacles between Mount Challenger and Crooked Thumb; rappel the route to reverse back to the glacier and camp.

before.approach: Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (end of FR 32, ~3,100 ft) on Trail #674. Climb steadily through forest for about 4 miles to Hannegan Pass (5,050 ft), then descend the climbers' path toward the Chilliwack River/Boundary Camp area (last reliable water for a while) before regaining elevation onto Easy Ridge, a long, partly brushy climbers' route past blueberry meadows and the old fire-lookout foundation/antenna remains atop Easy Peak. From Easy Ridge, contour toward Whatcom Peak's east flank to the infamous 'Imperfect Impasse' — a moat/cliff notch that often still holds snow well into summer and typically requires a short stretch of low 5th-class downclimbing or a scramble around/under a snow tunnel to cross; rope up if it looks insecure. Beyond the Impasse, climb snowfields (fog/whiteout is a real hazard here — parties have mistakenly headed for Whatcom's summit wall instead of the pass) up to Perfect Pass (~5,800 ft), the standard base camp below Whatcom Peak. Trailhead to camp is roughly 16 miles one-way with about 7,000 ft of cumulative gain — a full, long day (8-12+ hours) for a fast party, and worth splitting into two days for most. From Perfect Pass, the second-day approach crosses onto the Challenger Glacier: rope up for crevasse hazard, traverse east around Challenger Arm, and cross roughly 2.5-3 miles of upper glacier into Luna Cirque below the east side of Mt. Challenger's subsidiary summits. In lower-snow years a broken icefall blocks the direct line beneath Challenger's sub-peaks; most parties detour high above the first crevasse band (or backtrack to Challenger Arm for a lower line) to reach the base of Poltergeist Pinnacle's distinctive dike-streaked granite shield, the southernmost sub-summit between Challenger and Crooked Thumb.

weather.typical: Typical North Cascades high-alpine summer weather — stretches of stable, dry weather interrupted by fast-moving Pacific frontal systems that can bring sudden wind, rain, or snow at this elevation
weather.probability: Afternoon thunderstorms and rapid weather deterioration are a recognized North Cascades summer risk; given the multi-day remote approach, a fast-moving system can strand or seriously endanger a party

seasonal_hazards.exposure: High consequence: Grade III alpine rock on a slender, loose-rock pinnacle deep in the Pickets, multiple days from any road; any fall, injury, or objective hazard incident (rockfall, glacier fall) would require a prolonged self-rescue or NPS/SAR helicopter response given the extreme remoteness

avalanche.zone: N/A - route is climbed only in summer (Jul-Sep), after NWAC's winter/spring avalanche forecast season ends, and no dedicated NWAC zone covers the remote Northern Pickets; the operative snow hazard here is glacier crevasse fall, not slab avalanche

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: Significant — the standard approach crosses the Challenger Glacier, with crevasses on approach; roped travel and crevasse rescue competence are required

fitnessSpec.hiking: Multi-day (typically 2-3 days each way) off-trail and glaciated approach with significant elevation gain via routes like Hannegan Pass/Easy Ridge to Perfect Pass and across the Challenger Glacier; sustained high fitness required
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Heavy — multi-day glacier expedition load (rope, glacier/crevasse rescue kit, camping gear, alpine rock rack) typically 40-50+ lbs

partner_requirements.approachTime: 2-3 days to reach the base via the standard Perfect Pass / Challenger Glacier approach
requiredSkills: Roped glacier travel and crevasse rescue (Challenger Glacier crossing)
Confident traditional multipitch leading at 5.7 on an alpine tower
Comfort and routefinding judgment on loose rock
Off-trail alpine navigation in extremely remote terrain
Self-rescue capability — help is multiple days away
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Expert alpinist with prior Picket Range or comparably remote North Cascades expedition experience — not a route for a first big alpine outing

before.overview: Poltergeist Pinnacle is a slender granite tower immediately south of Mount Challenger's summit in the Northern Pickets — one of the last named summits in the range to see a first ascent. Its sole documented route, the East Face (Grade IV, 5.9), climbs a striking shield of dark granite streaked with white dikes via three pitches of sustained 5.8-5.9+ face and corner climbing (the first pitch, largely unprotected for its first ~40 feet, is the technical and psychological crux), followed by two long simul-climbed pitches up the connecting ridge to the summit.
before.permit: North Cascades NP complex: no permit for day climbs; all overnight backcountry stays require a backcountry permit (reserve on Recreation.gov or walk-up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center).

access.fees: $10/adult NPS wilderness camping fee (free under 16); the Perfect Pass/Whatcom Pass/Picket Range zone is walk-up only, so no $6 online reservation fee applies — a Northwest Forest Pass is also required to park at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead.
access.notes: 60% of sites are reservable in advance via Recreation.gov (2026 lottery Mar 2–13); the remaining 40% are walk-up, obtained in person the day before at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
access.rules: Leave No Trace; cross-country zone rules
access.permit: North Cascades NP wilderness permit required for overnight camping; Perfect Pass/Whatcom Pass/Picket Range is a walk-up-only cross-country zone with no advance reservation — permit must be obtained in person at a park Wilderness Information Center, typically no earlier than the day before departure.
access.land_manager: National Park Service — North Cascades National Park (Stephen Mather Wilderness)
access.passRequired: NPS backcountry wilderness permit + Northwest Forest Pass for trailhead parking

overnight_permit.what: North Cascades NP backcountry permit (cross-country zone), fee per person, not free
overnight_permit.where: Reserve on Recreation.gov, or get a walk-up permit in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center. Hannegan-side permits can also be picked up at the Glacier Public Service Center on its limited summer days.

before.beta: Established in August 2007 by Wayne Wallace and Mike Layton after a grueling approach, this route starts in the center of Spectre's south face and climbs about 800 feet of runout terrain into a 'deep, spooky' chimney that is completely enclosed inside the mountain at times, then continues on exposed face climbing past an offwidth section before a ridge traverse gains the summit. The route is noted for being largely devoid of crack protection through its runout sections.
watch_out: Extended runout climbing with little to no protection
Loose/exfoliating rock typical of Northern Pickets gneiss
A fully committing rappel sequence is required in places
Extremely remote — self-rescue would take days
hazards: Long runout pitches devoid of crack protection
Committing rappels with few options to bail
No cell service; multi-day approach makes rescue slow
before.rappels: No rappel descent is recorded for this wall: the first-ascent party downclimbed steep snow on Spectre's far side to a system of ledges and traversed around the mountain back to the south face. Carry anchor material anyway. This route's own hazard notes warn of committing rappels with few options to bail, and retreat off the upper, runout face is described as difficult given a near-total lack of gear placements - which is why the advice on file is to commit to the route rather than to plan on rappelling off it.

before.approach: Start at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead (elev. ~3,120 ft) at the end of Ruth Creek Road (FS-32). From the trailhead, follow the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail #674 gently up the Ruth Creek valley (views of Mt. Sefrit and Nooksack Ridge) for about 4 miles and roughly 2,000 ft of gain to 5,050 ft Hannegan Pass — this stretch is straightforward, well-graded, and has reliable water at Ruth Creek crossings for the first couple of miles. At the pass, leave the maintained trail: a boot path/climbers' route (watch for a cut-log marker at the unsigned junction — parties have noted the turnoff is easy to miss) breaks off toward Easy Ridge rather than continuing down to Boundary Camp/Chilliwack River. From here it is sustained cross-country travel: climb onto and follow Easy Ridge itself, a hot, dry, open, south-facing ridge crest with limited shade — flowing water is available relatively early on the ridge but the FA party warned this stretch 'would be brutal later in the season and in dry years.' Continue along/over Easy Peak (a common first bivy, roughly a full day, ~10 hours, from the trailhead) and then descend/traverse past the notch known as Imperfect Impasse, before regaining elevation to Challenger Col on the flank of Mt. Challenger. From Challenger Col, traverse the southern Challenger cirque (glacial terrain — rope/crevasse-awareness recommended near the pocket glacier) toward the west ridge of Phantom Peak, a typical second bivy site, avoiding lingering snow at Pickle Pass. From this high camp it is a further, mostly straightforward cross-country traverse across the western slopes to the base of Spectre Peak's south ridge, reached around sunrise on what is effectively day three. In total this is roughly a 46-mile, ~17,500 ft round-trip approach-and-climb outing (74 km), typically broken into 2 or more travel days each way with route-finding, glacier travel, and off-trail ridge scrambling throughout — this is genuinely one of the longest, most remote approaches in the North Cascades, not a simple hike-in.

pitch_detail.notes: Start up right of the entry notch: about 100 ft of 4th-class scrambling leads into 100 ft of 5.7 climbing up blocky terrain; some parties simul-climb this pitch to the first ledge.
Continue up low-fifth-class blocky ground to a large, tree-dotted ledge, then traverse left to gain the ridge crest proper.

The technical crux: climbs the cleaner face right of a prominent mossy gully, where roughly 10 ft of overhanging, chossy rock adds spice above sparse protection; the parallel gully itself offers a looser but more protectable fallback line.
Solid cracks and ledgy slabs lead up toward the crest on noticeably better rock than the pitches below.
Clean-walled climbing along a narrow, exposed knife-edge stretch of the ridge crest.
Continued crest climbing on generally solid gneiss to a stance below the ridge's gendarme band.

Follow the crest past a funky notch to the base of an imposing, shattered gendarme where the rock is sharp and loose enough to 'sing' when tapped; a roughly 25m rappel into the gap is followed by a self-belayed ascent of the far wall.
The route's best pitch: a clean 20-30 ft hands-and-fists crack gives genuinely fun, well-protected climbing to a belay alcove.
Steep, featured face climbing with abundant gear placements on solid rock.
Easier ground over heather ramps and blocky terrain, working back toward the ridge crest.
Traverse just below the crest for about 100 ft of low-fifth-class terrain on loose, gravel-covered rock -- careful footwork required.

Final technical pitch weaves through narrow, hoodoo-like towers of soft, chalky rock reminiscent of Utah's Fisher Towers; top out with a ~30m rappel from the last tower to a big grassy ledge, then downclimb roughly 600 ft of 3rd/4th-class terrain (with a couple of low-5th moves, roughly 5.0) to the summit.

rappel_detail.notes: Key technical rappel of the descent, from the final hoodoo tower down to a grassy ledge system, within the ~600 ft downclimb from the summit.
rappel_detail.anchor: natural gear anchor (no fixed anchors documented; horns/cracks/slung blocks)

rappel_detail.notes: Past an exposed gendarme roughly at the Pitch 7 band on the west side of the ridge.

itinerary.cal: Best done mid-to-late summer once Easy Ridge and Challenger Col are snow-free enough for the cross-country traverse; North Cascades NP backcountry permits are required for both bivy sites.

days.note: Hike from the Hannegan Pass Trailhead over Hannegan Pass and out along the Easy Ridge boundary trail/climbers' path, continuing past Easy Peak to a bivy. Long day on trail and open ridge with a big pack; water can be scarce late-season on the ridge crest.

days.objective: Reach a bivy site beyond Easy Peak via Hannegan Pass and Easy Ridge

days.note: Off-trail traverse dropping to Imperfect Impasse, up and over Challenger Col, then cross-country to a second bivy positioned below the west/south ridge of Phantom Peak, at the base of Spectre's South Ridge. Route-finding and some exposed scrambling on this leg.
days.title: Cross-country traverse to camp below Phantom Peak's south ridge
days.objective: Reach a bivy near the base of Phantom Peak's south ridge (Spectre's approach camp)

days.note: Alpine start from camp at first light, racking up at the base of the ridge. Twelve pitches of climbing (about 1,800 ft of pitched climbing plus 600 ft of simul-climbing) through a crux overhanging 5.9 choss section low on the route and a memorable band of narrow, hoodoo-like rock towers requiring an intermediate rappel, finishing with roughly 600 ft of 4th/low-5th class scrambling to the summit.

before.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb roughly 600 ft of 3rd-class terrain with a couple of low-5th-class moves (the FA party called the upper section 'glory 5.0 terrain') back down through the ridge's hoodoo/tower section. Within that section is the route's key rappel: a single ~30-meter rappel from the final hoodoo tower down to a grassy ledge system. A second, lower rappel of about 25 meters has also been reported past an exposed gendarme roughly at the Pitch 7 band on the west side of the ridge — parties should carry a single 60m rope (or two ropes) and be ready for up to two short technical rappels, though in some conditions the lower one can reportedly be avoided/downclimbed. No fixed anchors are documented on this obscure, first-ascent-era route; expect natural gear anchors (horns, cracks, slung blocks) rather than bolts, and back them up — this is remote, low-traffic terrain with essentially no fixed hardware. Below the rappels/downclimbing, the descent drops onto Spectre's east-facing slopes back toward the Challenger Col/Easy Ridge approach line; in the FA party's heavy-snow-year, early-season conditions this was continuous, 'super chill' steep snow (glissade-friendly with an ice axe and the usual steep-snow/glacier caution), letting them avoid the 'typical endless scree and loose talus' that this face otherwise holds in leaner, later-season conditions — parties visiting in a low-snow year or later in the season should expect a much looser, scree/talus descent instead of snow travel. From the base, retrace the approach line back over Challenger Col, past Imperfect Impasse, along Easy Ridge, over Hannegan Pass, and out the maintained trail to the Hannegan Pass Trailhead — effectively a full reversal of the multi-day approach, not a same-day walk-off.
before.rope_note: Northern Pickets, remote south face/ridge route: ~800ft of runout climbing into a chimney, a rappel into a notch, then exposed face climbing to a gendarme.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Very strenuous multi-day off-trail approach via Hannegan Pass and Easy Ridge to Challenger Col, including sustained cross-country travel and route-finding (Imperfect Impasse) before the climb even starts
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Heavy overnight pack for multi-day food/camp/rack on the approach, then a stripped-down summit-day pack for the Grade III climb itself

partner_requirements.approachTime: Multi-day (typically 2 days each way) via Hannegan Pass and Easy Ridge to a bivy below Phantom Peak's south ridge; build in a weather/rest day given the remoteness and difficulty of the approach
requiredSkills: Confident 5.9R traditional/alpine rock leading on loose, unfamiliar rock
Route-finding among towers with no fixed protection or established topo
Off-trail navigation and class 3-4 scrambling on the approach
Self-rescue and remote wilderness first aid
Efficient multi-pitch systems needed to complete a Grade III route in a day from a remote camp
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Experienced alpine rock climbers with prior committing North Cascades (ideally Pickets-caliber) objectives; must be self-sufficient with no realistic chance of a quick rescue

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Start point for the 2-day approach (Hannegan Pass -> Easy Ridge -> Pickell Pass) used on this route's first ascent.
waypoints.directions: Drive Forest Road 32, the Hannegan Pass Road, to its end at the Hannegan Pass Trailhead at about 3,120 ft. The road is normally open to the trailhead through summer and early fall but has a documented history of washout damage needing bypass construction, so confirm current status with the Glacier Public Service Center before driving in. Park with a Northwest Forest or interagency pass displayed; the overnight wilderness permit for everything past Hannegan Pass is a separate Park Service permit picked up in Glacier or Marblemount.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass
waypoints.note: High point of the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail (#674); stay on the maintained trail here and descend into the Chilliwack valley; the cross-country toward Easy Ridge starts far below, after the river ford, and the Copper Ridge trail branches down in the valley rather than at the pass.
waypoints.directions: Follow the maintained Hannegan Pass Trail #674 up the Ruth Creek valley, about 4 miles and roughly 2,000 ft of gain to the 5,050 ft pass, with Mount Sefrit and Nooksack Ridge across the valley. The grade is gentle and the tread is good the whole way, and the Ruth Creek crossings in the first couple of miles carry reliable water.

waypoints.name: Chilliwack River ford
waypoints.note: Ford the Chilliwack River below Easy Ridge on the climbers' path past Copper Creek before switchbacking back up; can be a cold, thigh-deep crossing in early season.
waypoints.directions: From the pass the maintained trail keeps going, and this is the stretch people get wrong: do not leave it here. Descend the switchbacks north-east into the Chilliwack valley, losing about 1,500 ft over roughly three miles to the Copper Creek area at a little over 3,000 ft, where the Copper Ridge trail branches away and is not your turn. Continue past it on the climbers' path and drop to the Chilliwack River ford below Easy Ridge. The crossing is cold and can run thigh-deep in early season, so pick a braided section, unclip your hipbelt, and cross before the afternoon melt comes down. The climbers' path switchbacks straight back up the far side, so this low point at 3,600 ft is the bottom of the whole approach.

waypoints.name: Bivy beyond Easy Peak
waypoints.note: Established climbers' bivy near the summit of Easy Peak (6,613'), reached via the Easy Ridge climbers' path gained above Hannegan Pass; typical end of day one.
waypoints.directions: From the river, switchback steeply back up onto Easy Ridge and then follow the crest itself. This is a hot, dry, open, south-facing ridge with almost no shade; flowing water shows up relatively early along it, but the first-ascent party warned this stretch would be brutal later in the season and in dry years, so fill up while you can. Continue along and over Easy Peak to the established bivy beyond it, roughly a ten-hour day with a full pack from the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Imperfect Impasse
waypoints.note: A notch on Easy Ridge that must be downclimbed and re-ascended to continue toward the Pickets proper; exposed and slower than it looks from a distance.
waypoints.directions: Leave camp and keep going along the ridge off-trail toward the Pickets, dropping to the cleft known as the Imperfect Impasse. This leg is route-finding and exposed scrambling rather than walking, and the notch has to be downclimbed and then re-ascended on the far side; parties consistently find it slower than it looks from a distance.

waypoints.name: Challenger Col
waypoints.note: Snow/glacier col that gains the western slope of the range; parties have noted a bergschrund forming near its top by mid-to-late season.
waypoints.directions: Out of the notch, regain elevation onto the flank of Mount Challenger and climb through Challenger Col. This is snow and glacier ground rather than rock, so rope up and treat it as crevassed terrain; parties have reported a bergschrund opening near the top of the col by mid to late season.

waypoints.name: Pickle Pass
waypoints.note: Gap below Spectre's serrated south ridge of hoodoos, visible from Frenzel Camp, where the technical climbing on the route begins.
waypoints.directions: From the col, traverse the southern Challenger cirque toward the west ridge of Phantom Peak, staying roped near the pocket glacier. Phantom's west and south ridge is the usual second bivy and where most parties stop for the night. Pickle Pass itself can hold snow well into the season, and the first-ascent party found it snowed over and skirted it rather than crossing.

waypoints.name: Spectre Peak
waypoints.directions: From the base of the south ridge, start up right of the entry notch: about 100 ft of fourth class leads into blocky 5.7 climbing, then low-fifth ground to a large tree-dotted ledge and a traverse left onto the crest proper. The crest gives sustained 5.4 to 5.8 climbing past the crux third pitch, a short overhanging band of 5.9 choss above sparse gear on the face right of a mossy gully, and past a shattered gendarme at pitch 7 where a 25 m rappel into the gap is followed by a self-belayed ascent of the far wall. The last pitch weaves through narrow, chalky hoodoo towers to a 30 m rappel off the final tower onto a big grassy ledge, from which about 600 ft of third and fourth class with a couple of low-fifth moves leads to the top.

weather.typical: Typical North Cascades summer alpine pattern: clear mornings with afternoon cloud buildup; the range is exposed to fast-moving frontal systems even in summer
weather.probability: Afternoon thundershowers possible, especially in a wetter month; a multi-day settled high is needed for an objective this remote and committing

seasonal_hazards.exposure: Sustained alpine rock exposure with loose rock and route-finding among towers; a fall or injury here is a serious self-rescue situation given the multi-day approach and remoteness

avalanche.zone: N/A - non-glaciated summer alpine rock route in the Southern Pickets; NWAC does not maintain a forecast zone specific to this area, and the route is climbed outside the active avalanche season

seasonal_hazards.crevasses: The South Route climbing itself is alpine rock, but the standard multi-day approach and return both cross glaciated terrain in the Challenger cirque (near the pocket glacier below Challenger Col) — rope/crevasse-awareness is recommended for this crossing.
